newsitem.title: FRANCE: France imposes 1998 spending freeze, output up. [CORRECTED 12:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: France imposes 1998 spending freeze, output up. [CORRECTED 12:00 GMT]

text.p: France's government ordered a public spending freeze for 1998 on Thursday as the opposition Socialists sought to woo voters ahead of a snap parliamentary election next month with a pledge of no new taxes.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe's office confirmed that ministers had been told to hold 1998 state spending unchanged in nominal terms for the second successive year, meaning a cut of more than one percent in real terms.

But it sought to offset the impression of austerity by trumpeting signs of an economic upturn ahead of the May 25-June 1 election to the National Assembly, likely to be dominated by the issues of unemployment, taxes and purchasing power.

"Growth is taking off again," Budget Minister Alain Lamassoure said, pointing to what he called robust industrial production figures. He said France might make more tax cuts than planned if economic growth exceeded forecasts for 1997.
The Socialists accused the centre-right coalition of trying to secure re-election before imposing draconian new austerity measures to help qualify for a single European currency.

"We will not raise taxes," Martine (Corrects to add first name) Aubry, a member of the Socialist leadership, said in an RTL radio interview. The Socialists say they favour the single currency, but not at the price of a further bout of austerity.

"We will simply make a better share-out between (the tax burden on) income from capital and income from salaries, we will relaunch consumer spending and we will introduce a new model of development," she said.

Juppe and Socialist leader Lionel Jospin were to hold their first public rallies later on Thursday in what is likely to be a short but bruising campaign after President Jacques Chirac risked his political career by dissolving parliament on Monday.

Aubry said the prime minister was bowing to demands for strict austerity to meet the Maastricht Treaty budget criteria for a single European currency -- a deficit of less than three percent of gross domestic product.

Aubry, daughter of former European Commission president Jacques Delors who was an architect of the treaty, said the three percent target "is not the Bible...the treaty itself says that the trend must be taken into account".
Finance Minister Jean Arthuis denied media reports that the budget faced a slippage because of a tax revenue shortfall.
"Nothing points to slippage in the state budget," he told the business daily Les Echos.

In their first meetings with ordinary voters since the campaign kicked off, Juppe was to travel to the rough and tumble Mediterranean port of Marseille, while Jospin planned to tour several troubled outer Paris suburbs.
Surveys show voters' concerns are dominated by unemployment, at a post-war record of 12.8 percent.

The first opinion poll taken since Chirac called the election suggested the ruling centre-right would win comfortably, but with a sharply reduced majority in the National Assembly, where it now holds 80 percent of the seats.
But another survey found most voters expected to be hit by further austerity measures after the election.

In a reminder of nagging labour unrest since unions brought France to a virtual standstill for 24 days in late 1995 to protest at government policies, a one-day strike by train conductors over wage demands cut rail services to about a third of normal in many parts of France.
Francois Leotard, head of the Union for French Democracy (UDF) which is the junior partner in the ruling coalition, said he wanted Chirac to get involved in the campaign.
"The tradition...is that the president at some point indicates the choice he is advising for the French people," he said. Chirac is meant to be aloof from day-to-day politics. 240942 GMT apr 97
